title: CONGENITAL MYOPATHY 10B, MILD VARIANT
alt_titles: MYOPATHY, AREFLEXIA, RESPIRATORY DISTRESS, AND DYSPHAGIA, EARLY-ONSET, MILD VARIANT

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that the mild variant of congenital myopathy-10 (CMYO10B) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEGF10 gene (612453) on chromosome 5q23.

checks.claim: The mild variant of congenital myopathy-10 (CMYO10B) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEGF10 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: patients displaying a less severe phenotype, with later respiratory failure and minicores on muscle biopsy (mvEMARDD or with minicore myopathy), harbour homozygous or compound heterozygous missense variants affecting the cysteine in the EGF-like domain
checks.explanation: The paper links the mild variant to homozygous or compound heterozygous MEGF10 variants.

checks.claim: The MEGF10 gene is located on chromosome 5q23.
checks.evidence_quote: MEGF10 lies within a linkage peak on chromosome 5 that reached the maximum possible LOD score of 1.329.
checks.explanation: The paper gives chromosome 5 only, not the band 5q23. Treating 5q23 as standard nomenclature is acceptable.

paragraphs.text: Takayama et al. (2016) noted that MEGF10 mutations cause early-onset myopathy with areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD), and also a milder phenotype, minicore myopathy. Croci et al. (2022) described the MEGF10-related phenotypic spectrum as variable. At the severe end are infantile forms in which patients are ventilator-dependent and die in childhood. At the milder end are chronic disorders with a more favorable course and later onset, classified as the mild variant (mvEMARDD). Patients with the mild variant may have only very mild muscle weakness and mild respiratory dysfunction, and some, but not all, have minicores on muscle biopsy.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) reported a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an autosomal recessive myopathy. Weakness appeared by 12 months of age, first in the neck. It was present throughout the body but was mainly axial and proximal, and it stabilized in adolescence. Facial weakness was also present. Neck contractures were seen in infancy, and contractures of the elbows, knees, and heel cords had developed by adulthood. Serum creatine kinase measured before age 10 years was mildly elevated. All 3 patients had childhood-onset scoliosis treated with spinal fusion. Beginning at age 10 to 11 years, all developed respiratory problems treated with nighttime bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation. One patient was born with a cleft palate that was surgically repaired. A second had a midline ridge on her palate in adulthood and tended to reflux liquids into her nose. All 3 had hypernasal speech. Muscle biopsies showed dystrophic features: myofibers replaced by fatty tissue, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers. They also showed moth-eaten fibers and minicores, which suggested a congenital myopathy. Rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, central cores, nemaline rods, and ragged red fibers were absent. Type I fibers slightly predominated and varied more in size than type II fibers. Before genetic testing, the diagnosis had been given as limb-girdle muscular dystrophy or spinal muscular atrophy.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) also described a Caucasian girl with distant Portuguese ancestry (subject 105-1) who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease; no other family member was affected. At several weeks of age she had hypotonia, first seen as a weak neck and floppy head. Other early findings were a markedly high-arched palate, failure to thrive due to poor feeding, blue-tinged sclerae, and hyperflexible joints. As a child she had frequent acute pulmonary infections but no chronic breathing problems, and she breathed unassisted at night. Serum creatine kinase at age 10 years was mildly elevated at 302 U/L. Mild scoliosis noted at that age had progressed to 20 degrees by age 12 years. Throughout childhood she had mild, nonprogressive, mainly proximal weakness, including facial weakness. Muscle biopsy showed marked variation in fiber size, internalized nuclei, slightly increased endomysial connective tissue, and patches of decreased NADH activity. Electron microscopy confirmed minicores.

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man born to healthy consanguineous parents. He was born at 33 weeks' gestation, needed resuscitation for asphyxia, and had a weak suck. From the first months of life he had a congenital myopathic phenotype with elbow contractures and scoliosis. He had no motor developmental delay or intellectual disability. He developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia, and respiratory involvement, and needed nocturnal noninvasive ventilation from age 16 years. Examination showed axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy and weakness, preserved facial expression, cleft palate, global areflexia, and bilateral contractures of the elbows and ankles. He walked without support with an equinovarus-supinated foot stance, hyperlordosis, and pelvic tilt, but needed a manual wheelchair for longer trips. He underwent bilateral Achilles tendon tenotomy and vertebral arthrodesis. From age 17 years he had swallowing difficulties and recurrent pulmonary infections due to aspiration of food. Brain and spine MRI, ECG, echocardiogram, and serum creatine kinase were normal. Motor and sensory conduction was normal apart from reduced amplitude of the muscle evoked potential, and sensation was not impaired. A first muscle biopsy at age 5 years showed nonspecific changes: variation in fiber size, internal nuclei, and fibrosis. A later biopsy showed myofibrillar alterations, including whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions, and minicores.

paragraphs.text: In the 3 affected sibs of family 1030 with a congenital myopathy with minicores, Boyden et al. (2012) combined linkage data with whole genome sequencing. They identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the MEGF10 gene: C326R and C774R. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mutations were in trans and segregated with the disorder in all 6 family members. Both mutations were absent from dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, and the NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project data, and from 715 and 645 genotyped controls, respectively. Each changes a cysteine in an atypical EGF-like domain that is conserved in 43 species, and the authors expected the changes to disrupt disulfide bonds. Morpholino knockdown of megf10 in zebrafish caused myopathic phenotypes, which the authors took as support for the pathogenicity of the human mutations.

paragraphs.text: In a 22-year-old Italian man with a progressive form of mild-variant EMARDD, born to consanguineous parents, Croci et al. (2022) identified a homozygous c.2096G-C transversion (NM_001256545.2) in the MEGF10 gene, resulting in a cys699-to-ser (C699S) substitution at a conserved cysteine in an EGF-like domain. The mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing; both parents were heterozygous carriers. It was absent from ClinVar and gnomAD and was predicted to be damaging by several in silico tools.
